We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) has become so popular that most modern headphones, budget-friendly or otherwise, include it in some form. It uses both the headset's microphones and speakers to create a noise-canceling barrier. Its effectiveness depends on the device's execution and whether it fits snugly over your head.

You don't need to pay a premium for state-of-the-art headsets; cheaper alternatives are well-made and do a great job with ANC. With high-budget, mid-range, and entry-level ANC headphones, people with different budgets can check out some of the best options on the market. The sheer number of headsets on the market can make this feel daunting, but these recommendations should help you get started.

Sony's flagship headphones keep impressing, with the Sony WH-1000XM6 adding another stellar entry to a lineup praised across the board for its incredible noise cancellation. Sound quality received similar compliments. What Hi-Fi? noted that the expanded soundstage did justice to these headphones' dynamic, detailed audio. GearLab highlighted the headset's excellent high- and low-frequency output. Another area where the XM6s excel is call quality, as multiple critics noted. SoundGuys highlighted the quality of this device's microphones, which may be why the ANC is so competent.

$458 isn't exactly cheap, so the discounted rate of $378 at the time of writing is a welcome reprieve for an audiophile's wallet if they need a good pair of noise-canceling headphones right now. That noted, for an expensive pair of headphones, some features are missing that are worth considering. For starters, they have no ingress protection (IP) rating, so taking them to risky environments like the beach or the pool is out of the question. Since most people will use the XM6s for wireless listening, the lack of aptX HD support is a notable disappointment.

Speaking of expensive headphones, the Apple AirPods Max 2 is obviously a great option for people who use multiple devices in the Apple ecosystem. Just turn on Pairing Mode to automatically connect to any nearby Apple device, then adjust settings in the Settings menu. This includes a personalized spatial audio setting and Live Translation. Even for Windows or Android users, this headset is worth it, despite the $449.99 price tag and limited access to some features.

Critics praised the noise cancellation, calling it a notable improvement over the previous model in their tests. Transparency mode received similar praise. Another improvement over the previous model is a higher-quality amplifier and the H2 chip, both of which play a major role in unlocking audio fidelity that wowed many critics.

According to recent reports, however, despite its achievements, the AirPods Max 2 has two major drawbacks. The lack of a user-adjustable equalizer is puzzling, even though Apple is confident its adaptive EQ can do the job. Another area where these headphones failed to impress critics is battery life. In PCMag's tests, it lasted 20 hours with ANC on, nowhere near what its rivals can achieve. In fact, they noted that this battery life is similar to that of the previous model, which isn't great.

Any pair of headphones universally praised for their noise cancellation is clearly doing something right. The 2nd Gen Bose QuietComfort Ultra nails it. The headphones' overall sound profile also drew largely positive reception. What Hi-Fi? loved the soundscape these headphones project, while PCMag appreciated how clear the audio was without sacrificing bass. They were similarly impressed with the headphones' 30-hour battery life, but there's a catch. Whether you use the 3.5-millimeter jack or the USB-C port, which supports lossless audio, the headset still runs on battery, which is odd.

Sources indicate that what Hi-Fi? praised the ergonomic folding design, while PCMag noted that the metal frame and high-quality plastic housing improved the headset's build quality. They found its clamping force and padded earcups very comfortable. Unfortunately, like most other over-ear headphones, this headset lacks an IP rating. The equalizer you can tweak in the Bose app isn't anything to write home about, either. The $449 price tag can be hard to stomach, but you can save 20 percent with the current discount, bringing the price down to $359.99.

Industry observers note that one of the most expensive headphones on this list, you might as well steer clear of the Sony 1000X The Collexion headset if the previous devices already strained your wallet. For what it's worth, Sony tries to justify its $648 price tag, though whether it succeeds is another matter.

Sources indicate that reviewers praised the audio quality, with What Hi-Fi? finding the audio's level of detail and spaciousness quite immersive. At 11.3 ounces, it may feel heavy, but reviewers found the overall fit comfortable. As expected, ANC was another area where the 1000X wowed multiple critics.

In a recent development, unfortunately, this headset gets a few things wrong, which keeps it from being an easy recommendation. People expect excellent performance from headphones that cost this much, but Sony stumbled a bit in execution. What Hi-Fi? noticed that the headphones' exterior was a fingerprint magnet and looked rather shabby after extended use. Multiple reviewers also noted that the 24-hour battery life with ANC on fell short of competitors' 30-hour standard.

In a recent development, if you want budget-friendly headphones with solid ANC, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 is a strong option. Reviewers noted that this $129.99 device punched above its weight, delivering satisfying ANC, though CNET felt there was room for improvement. SoundGuys also noted that the audio felt off when noise cancellation was on. Speaking of which, reviewers praised this device's sound quality, but with a few caveats. SoundGuys found the headphones' frequency response odd, while CNET noted that 3D Sound mode completely tanked audio quality.

One of the Soundcore Space 2's strongest features is its battery life. The manufacturer confidently claims it can last 70 hours without ANC, although noise cancellation slashes that to 50 hours, which is still excellent. PCMag also loved the in-depth equalizer in the Soundcore app. CNET noticed that this headset did a good job of reducing background noise during calls. In fact, they mentioned it was a bit too effective, to the point that the speaker's voice itself sounded muted.

According to recent reports, at $479, the Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3 faces stiff competition. The Apple AirPods Max 2, Sony WH-1000XM6, and 2nd-Gen Bose QuietComfort Ultra all cost about the same, so the PX7 S3 needs to do a lot to stand out against these reliable headphones. For what it's worth, reviews are largely positive. They nailed the ANC, in their eyes, to the point that T3 called it one of the biggest upgrades in this new and improved headset.

Many of the PX7 S3's post-launch features didn't sit well with critics, even though new owners can buy the device and enjoy promised features out of the gate, such as Spatial Audio. The 2-band EQ at launch didn't impress SoundGuys, so adding a new 5-band EQ is a welcome change. Ultimately, sound quality is one aspect that thoroughly impressed reviewers. What Hi-Fi? praised the full-bodied, detailed audio output, while T3 were fans of the powerful sound these headphones deliver. It's arguably one of the best Bluetooth headphones for audiophiles.

Build quality was largely praised by critics too, who highlighted the textured fabric of its headband, a slimmer build compared to previous models, and an Annular Guard design — a series of small openings circling each earcup — that is made to prevent any wind noise while also adding a touch of elegance to the PX7 S3's looks. However, this new design didn't fit well for many reviewers, and the lack of a foldable design is a glaring miss.

At $149.99, the Baseus Inspire XH1 is already on the cheaper side of this list. Add a $50 discount, and you can snag this decent pair of budget headphones for just $99.99. That makes them one of the best value-for-money headphones you can get, with BGR claiming they can outperform competitors priced around $250. Multiple reviewers attest to its sound quality, which the default "Sound by Bose" audio preset certainly helps. This mode delivers great bass, upper-mids, and high frequencies. The same isn't true of the two Dolby Audio presets, Music and Cinema, which failed to impress critics.

According to recent reports, critics liked the noise cancellation, but it comes with a catch. Critics noticed that audio quality suffers as soon as you turn on ANC, which limits its usability. In our review, we found the noise cancellation to be the one major flaw holding these headphones back. Digital Trends also wasn't a huge fan of the headset's audio transparency. To keep the price down, Baseus left out wear detection, a bare-minimum feature many headphones offer. One thing that did impress critics about this headset is its amazing battery life. The Inspire XH1 can last 100 hours on a full charge with ANC off. That number drops to 65 hours with noise cancellation, which is still more than enough for most owners.

Overall, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless is a decent pair of headphones for $399.99. Reviewers liked the sound — Trusted Reviews praised the tonally rich audio, while What Hi-Fi? was a fan of the refined sound presentation. The midrange also sounded very impressive in their tests. The noise cancellation is where things get tricky. SoundGuys noted decent ANC, but Trusted Reviews noted its struggles in noisy environments.

Several other reasons make the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless worth buying. The manufacturer claims a 57-hour battery life, and the best part is that you can replace the unit if it starts nearing the end of its lifespan. Reviewers also heaped praise on the build quality. It's far more minimalist than previous models, with metallic accents adding a premium touch. Critics say the large earcups are comfortable enough for long sessions, though the fact that the device doesn't fold entirely makes it a bit of a pain to carry around. Don't expect an IP rating if you're hoping to go for a swim with the Momentum 5 Wireless wrapped snugly around your head.

It has been revealed that most people know Sonos for its stellar home theater music systems. The Sonos Arc Ultra is arguably the best soundbar on the market, and pairing it with a Sub 4 and two Era 300 speakers completes your home theater audio setup. However, their headphones have been playing catch-up to the best major headphone brands for a while. PCMag noted that the Sonos Ace Ultra made major strides in audio performance, but they, along with other reviewers, couldn't help but agree it put itself in a tough spot at $449. The competition is fierce, to the point that critics feel the Arc Ultra is outperformed in both sound quality and ANC.

Even people deep in the Sonos ecosystem will find this headset a hard sell, with T3 noting that its integration with other Sonos products isn't great. The UI buries the Arc Ultra's settings in the app, making them hard to find. That said, reviewers were impressed by the sound quality. PCMag appreciated the warm audio response, while What Hi-Fi? found the sound output rich and powerful, especially in the bass. ANC gets the job done for most critics, and they called the sleek, comfortable design the cherry on top. In fact, this improved ANC sealed the deal for us in our review of the Sonos Ace Ultra.

Sources indicate that the Nothing Headphone (a) is yet another good option for anyone seeking out a budget-friendly pair of noise-canceling headphones. The company is known for its unique, transparent design, and the Headphone (a) pulls no punches with a polarizing look that owners will either love or hate. It's fantastic value for $199, and a cheaper $130.99 price tag at the time of writing makes it an even more tantalizing proposition. At this price, we consider it the best headphones you can buy. Battery life was also universally praised by critics, with the Headphone (a) running for almost 75 hours with ANC on. Speaking of which, critics largely praised the noise cancellation, though there are some caveats. PCMag noted that strong winds negatively affected the ANC, while Mashable wasn't too impressed with the headphone's noise-canceling capabilities.

Sound quality is also mixed, if reviewers are to be believed. It was mostly praised by reviewers, with TechRadar stating that this headset is a notable upgrade over the Headphone (a). However, PCMag wasn't a huge fan of the bass-heavy audio presentation, and SoundGuys wasn't a huge fan of the stock sound tuning. While the design itself may not be to your taste, comfort is one area where the Headphone (a) won't disappoint. Critics appreciated the plastic build, which cut unnecessary weight and made the headset easier to carry around. The ear cushions also help here, but PCMag noted they aren't as well-made as those on the Headphone (1).

Recent findings suggest that to ensure high-quality recommendations, all noise-canceling headphones on this list have strong review scores — such as 4 out of 5, 8 out of 10, or 80 out of 100 — from three or more reputable publications. The only exception is a qualitative positive recommendation from BGR for the Baseus Inspire XH1. Aside from this website, the other review outlets we've chosen include TechRadar, Trusted Reviews, CNET, Wired, PCMag, Mashable, Digital Trends, SoundGuys, What Hi-Fi?, GearLab, and T3.

Industry observers note that LG describes robotics as a future growth business built on physical AI, or AI embodied in machines operating in real-world settings. Its approach combines robot platforms, robot intelligence and data capabilities.

Sources indicate that its lineup spans industrial and commercial robots and is expanding into home robots. LG also develops and manufactures core components including actuators, while LG Data Factory collects and manages the large-scale data needed for robot training and operation.

Sources indicate that an image released with the announcement indicates CLOiD learning a washing-machine manufacturing process at LG Data Factory in August 2026. In a recent development, the agreement gives LG a formal evaluation path while the certification center’s systems and related standards are still being developed. CSS-Tricks, Version 20

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks.
  • It has been revealed that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time.
  • Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

It has been revealed that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the newly introduced v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

For example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

It has been revealed that yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:.

It has been revealed that for years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a fresh terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention promptly. Very happy here.

Oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

According to recent reports, the previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

It has been revealed that there are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really key, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

According to recent reports, I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

In a recent development, are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

Recent findings suggest that for example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

But this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

According to recent reports, oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

But I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

According to recent reports, what hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the new theme over the previous one.

Recent findings suggest that I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

Sources indicate that sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:.

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:.

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:.

The differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:.

Recent findings suggest that so, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:.

I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

Recent findings suggest that now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go quickly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

According to recent reports, this is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

Again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the latest layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

In a recent development, it’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

This one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

According to recent reports, using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more important things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

Industry observers note that oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

Industry observers note that there’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!

Recent findings suggest that mulching blades differ from regular blades in the way they handle the grass — they recirculate clippings, meaning they get more cuts. This makes them less effective for regular mowing, and despite installing upcoming blades taking merely five minutes, some homeowners simply may not like the mess that mulching apparatus leaves behind. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Investing in a home solar array became less attractive when the federal tax credit on energy-efficient installations ended in 2025. Even as panel production prices (for all different types of consumer solar panels) have continued to fall, the average quote for even a modest build in the United States can push above $20,000. As the leading state in solar projects, California has been at the brunt of a further decrease in returns as the Net Energy Metering 3.0 scheme in 2023 reduced prices for midday solar generation in the hopes of getting more residential battery projects into gear to supply the evening peak hours.

Industry observers note that A new wave of tariffs coming into effect in December will establish high floor prices on a key solar panel component, potentially pushing the breakeven period of a solar-only installation right up to if not past its typical useful life. As states have migrated their solar-based credit and rebate programs towards battery generation events, you're probably better off going with a solar and battery project for your home than a pure solar one.

Industry observers note that solar marketplace research firm EnergySage presently estimates project breakeven points running between 8 years in a state like California to 24 years in Alabama for an average-size build respective to each state. Many states fall within the 10- to 15-year timeframe, including Illinois, New York, Pennsylvania, and Texas. Keep in mind that these panels have an expected lifespan of anywhere between 20 and 35 years, depending on how new the installation is. These calculations do not include any applicable solar installation incentives, such as they are available from states.

Expect to wait longer for your payback if you're installing after December 4 as a wave of so-called Section 232 tariffs (which have also been used against steel and other metals used in home improvement tools from the likes of DeWalt and Craftsman) issued in August concerning polysilicon, a key component of photovoltaic panels, comes into effect. Imports of finished solar modules will be subject to a minimum sale price of 38 cents per watt plus a value-added tax of up to 15%.

In a recent development, disregarding the VAT, this represents a 20% to 50% increase from today's prices at common sources. Installers could decide to cut their non-fungible overhead — elements including labor, marketing, and margin that make up nearly half of the bill, according to EnergySage — to pass on a lower increase, at least initially. Still, even a single-digit percentage premium could mean an extra $1,000 or $2,000 to your bill.

Many states and utilities now offer installation and generation incentives for residential stored power projects. For example, energy providers in Massachusetts offer up to $1,375 a year for up to 60 summertime activations at 5kW output. In neighboring Rhode Island, the state will rebate builds at $250 per kilowatt-hour ($500 for property owners with eligible incomes) for the first 25kW of capacity and $175/kWh for further capacity on larger plots up to 250kW.

Tesla's Powerwall series of batteries are a go-to choice (though not the only one) for many proprietors and can make sense as part of an integrated setup with a smaller solar array for about the same price as going solar-only. You'll want to evaluate your own usage, brush up on incentive programs available to you, and then match those specs to products on the market to maximize your potential returns. This is all on top of the extra breathing room and peace of mind you get if and when a grid outage occurs — keeping the fridge running means you can tack on a trip's worth of groceries to your overall savings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A systematic review and meta-analysis by Bijay Bastola and colleagues, published November 16, 2026, in BMC Cardiovascular Disorders, estimated a pooled diagnostic-quality echocardiography yield of 96.3% for novice and nonexpert operators using real-time AI guidance across eight studies. The measure reflects whether an acquisition met each study’s predefined adequacy threshold.

Results diverged sharply by deployment. Six studies conducted under controlled or structured conditions produced a pooled yield of 98.0%, with a 95% confidence interval of 96.7% to 99.2%. Two decentralized, real-world community studies pooled to 63.7%, with a 95% confidence interval of 20.6% to 92.6%; their individual yields were 44.8% and 79.8%. A meta-regression found the subgroup difference statistically significant at p < 0.001.

Industry observers note that the authors treated that comparison as post hoc and exploratory, not preregistered. Deployment setting was intertwined with supervision, training, operator backgrounds, patient selection and outcome definitions, so the analysis does not establish setting as the cause. With only two community studies, the lower estimate is descriptive rather than a predictable success rate for future programs.

The analysis covered 2,365 examination-, scan-, or image-level observations acquired by 74 operators who had no prior formal echocardiography training or certification. Eligible studies involved real patients and AI guidance during acquisition itself, not automated interpretation of images captured earlier. The evidence spanned five AI systems and multiple operator types, from nurses and non-clinical research staff to medical trainees, general practitioners and community health workers.

Two reviewers independently searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, Embase, Scopus and ClinicalTrials.gov, with the final patch on September 27, 2026. A second statistical model estimated an overall yield of 93.0%; sensitivity checks using different study sets, outcome definitions and statistical methods ranged from 91.2% to 97.8%. The principal estimate’s 95% confidence interval was 85.5% to 99.3%, and substantial differences between studies led the authors to warn against treating the overall estimate as a universal yield for new deployments.

Independent expert readers judged image adequacy in five studies. The other three defined adequacy as the AI software successfully generating an automated left ventricular ejection fraction readout, a measure of heart function, so the system being evaluated also determined the outcome. Not every observation represented a separate patient: six studies reported examinations, one counted 60 scan attempts in 10 patients, and another counted 954 images from 159 patients.

Recent findings suggest that because nearly all included studies were single-arm, the results show what novices achieved with AI guidance rather than how much the guidance added over unaided acquisition. Diagnostic-quality acquisition also is not equivalent to an accurate diagnosis, and none of the studies reported effects on clinical management or patient outcomes.

The reviewers identified operator training, supervision, image-quality checks and quality assurance as priorities for wider deployment, and called for comparative real-patient studies linking image adequacy to diagnostic accuracy and outcomes. For screening programs, the practical implication is that trained nonexperts can feasibly acquire images under structured protocols, while broader deployment still needs evidence that reliable acquisition can be reproduced in community settings and that the resulting images lead to accurate diagnoses and improved patient outcomes.

#414. Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • Recent findings suggest that when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • Recent findings suggest that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

Recent findings suggest that when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Recent findings suggest that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

Recent findings suggest that frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

Sources indicate that CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Industry observers note that still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the manufacturer I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

Recent findings suggest that before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the company I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

Sources indicate that these questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional company I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

Wheelman isn’t an ordinary company, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the organization, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

It has been revealed that let’s imagine I’m designing a fresh landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

According to recent reports, only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

It has been revealed that wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

It has been revealed that I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Sources indicate that dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

Using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

Industry observers note that the modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

In a recent development, the result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

Industry observers note that one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

Wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

In a recent development, I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Sources indicate that combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

The point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same manufacturer.

Sources indicate that twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

It has been revealed that wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

And this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

Sources indicate that that’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

Do Electric Tankless Water Heaters Work As Well As Gas?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tankless water heaters are, as the name suggests, household appliances that provide hot water on demand without relying on a storage tank.
  • Sources indicate that there are two main types of tankless water heaters: gas-powered and electric.
  • Gas tankless water heaters also have the advantage during cooler months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tankless water heaters are, as the name suggests, household appliances that provide hot water on demand without relying on a storage tank. They work by bringing cold water into the device's heat exchanger, where it rapidly increases in temperature and comes out the other end as hot water. Tankless water heaters have a few drawbacks, from higher upfront installation costs to reduced performance in cold temperatures, but are arguably better than conventional tank-style heaters in several ways. Because these devices heat water on demand, owners will technically never run out of hot water. Plus, they're more energy efficient, take up less space, and have a longer lifespan, capable of lasting 20 years with proper maintenance. For the right house, a tankless water heater is a worthwhile upgrade.

Sources indicate that there are two main types of tankless water heaters: gas-powered and electric. While both perform well, gas models are generally better. The main reason is that gas tankless water heaters can deliver higher hot-water flow rates than electric models. Flow rate is the amount of water being discharged, measured in gallons per minute (GPM). Depending on the model, a gas-powered unit can deliver 4.5 GPM, plenty to support showers, faucets, and other appliances simultaneously, all without being super taxing on electrical systems.

Gas tankless water heaters also have the advantage during cooler months. Gas heaters have burner capacities ranging from 140,000 to 199,000 Btu/h. By comparison, residential electric heaters have roughly equivalent capacities of 47,770 to 109,100 Btu/h (14 to 32 kW). This means that gas tankless models have a higher heating capacity to raise the temperature of incoming water to the desired level.

Overall costs play a huge role when buying a water heater. Upfront, gas heaters are more expensive. A typical gas model will run you $1,160 on average, and that doesn't account for installation costs. Electric heaters, on the other hand, will cost you an average of $650. That may sound great, but operating costs are higher. Many electric units require a minimum of 120 amps and multiple 240V circuits to run— that's a lot of power. To put that into perspective, a conventional electric tank water heater only needs 18.8 amps at 240V. If your house can't provide enough power, then you'll need to upgrade the electrical panel. And a full panel upgrade can cost up to $2,000.

In a recent development, the environment also plays an vital role, as colder climates are harder on electric heaters. An electrical unit rated at 5GPM might only output 3GPM if it has to heat up cold groundwater and the power demand is high. A high-powered 36 kW unit will need to draw in 150 amps to heat up water by 80 degrees Fahrenheit. That is a ton of energy, and it puts a lot of pressure on a house's electrical infrastructure.

According to recent reports, back in 2019, Consumer Reports tested gas and electric tankless water heaters. They found that when the incoming water was warm at 74 degrees Fahrenheit, both the gas and electric models were able to heat and maintain the water. However, when the water was 58 degrees Fahrenheit, the electric unit struggled to deliver. It's for this reason that electric heaters are recommended for mild climates where the groundwater is warmer.

It has been revealed that despite their shortcomings, there are still some scenarios where an electric tankless water heater is a better option than a gas unit. For example, small living spaces or households that don't utilize a lot of hot water for appliances are perfect. Demand in these locations is low, so an electric heater won't be too taxing on your home's electrical or water systems. Also, these machines work better in warmer climates.

Although gas-powered heaters perform better in colder months, they still perform well during warmer weather. It's just that the gap between gas and electric is much smaller. Warm climates have warmer groundwater, which means that the machines can use less energy to heat water. Electric units are better in this scenario because they are cheaper upfront. Additionally, gas water heaters produce exhaust and need a ventilation system. With electric units, that's not an concern.

Garage doors are subject to a number of common problems, and a number of them concern the springs. Because they're tasked with counterbalancing the weight of the door itself, which can be tremendously heavy, a garage door's springs endure a lot of tension and occasionally need to be fully replaced. Don't worry: replacing a spring is considerably less expensive than replacing an entire garage door system.

Recent findings suggest that typically, replacing a spring will cost between $150 and $350 based on nationwide averages, most commonly landing close to $250. Prices will vary based on the type of spring. Torsion springs, which are the ones mounted above the opening of the metal shaft, are slightly more expensive, at around $75 to $150, while extension springs, the horizontal springs along the side tracks, are cheaper, around $50 to $100 per.

The remainder of the cost is labor, which will also vary by installer and by the number of springs you need replaced, but you can expect to pay between $75 and $150. While the cost isn't insignificant, replacing garage door springs is one of several home improvement projects you really should leave to the professionals.

According to recent reports, there are some methods for extending the life of your springs, like spraying them down with the best lubricant for garage doors, which coats them in a thin film that will help protect them. When the time does come to replace them, however, the installer will likely advise replacing both matching springs at the same time.

Paired springs that were installed at the same time will have endured the same number of lift cycles and roughly the same amount of wear cross their lifespan. This means that the partner of a failed spring will also be pretty likely to fail around the same time; knock out both at once and you can save yourself making a second call soon after. It may also save you on things like service fees that get charged per visit regardless of labor.

As to why you should let a pro handle your spring replacement, it's primarily a safety matter. A typical garage door can weigh upwards of several hundred pounds, and that weight puts the springs under incredible mechanical tension. Without the specialized tools in a professional installer's kit, messing with those springs can lead to sudden, violent release, which can cause severe injury or property damage. A certified pro has the training and equipment to safely uncoil or adjust a spring without risking harm, or damage to your garage or vehicle.

When Samsung ended its partnership with OneDrive as default cloud storage, it replaced it with Google storage, giving me a solid reason to consider going back to the Samsung Gallery app.

I've tested the Google storage integration, and I realized how invaluable it is, and now it's starting to win me back to Samsung Gallery.

I love how well Samsung Gallery runs on Galaxy devices, as it is snappy and works fantastically even offline.

However, it was always held back by its cloud backup tool: OneDrive.

Rather than tying into Google, it used OneDrive for years, which made it less ideal since most users have Google storage linked to their Android account.

In my case, I also had little reason to rely on OneDrive, as I use Google Workspace from Gmail to office tools like Docs and Sheets over Microsoft's suite.

Samsung Gallery is an incredible platform, held back only by OneDrive. It's the last remaining thorn that has always pushed me toward Google Photos on my Samsung devices.

But now that OneDrive is out of the picture, I have more reason to ditch Google Photos for Samsung Gallery.

It didn't take long for them to pick Google as the replacement for the Gallery.

According to recent reports, the integration was recently rolled out to supported devices, arriving alongside One UI 9. Even better, the setup is just as seamless as it was with OneDrive.

Plus, Google One offers a larger free tier at 15GB than OneDrive, which typically starts at 5GB and only expands when bundled with other perks.

In the Gallery app, there's a dedicated setting that lets you configure your backup using Google storage.

Open the cloud settings and pick the Google account you want to sync; it reveals all the Google profiles presently logged in to your Samsung device.

That requires minimal effort compared to dealing with Microsoft or creating a separate account just to start syncing with OneDrive.

I also ensured that the same Samsung account was active and logged in on the phone I wanted to use.

When configured, it automatically backs up my photos and videos.

There's a minor quirk after you've set it up: you can't easily switch Google accounts after you finish setup.

It requires turning off sync and removing the account from your Samsung device, and setting it up again.

I wish this could be remedied in the future without the added hurdle when switching Google profiles.

It always makes sense to stick with Google storage on Samsung hardware, and it removes the need to use Google Photos while my media still syncs automatically.

Direct cloud storage makes it easy to skip Google Photos and manage my Samsung photos and videos in the Gallery app.

Another thing I like is cross-device sync, so I can view and access my media on my Galaxy tablet or Galaxy Z Flip, and vice versa.

There's also an easier way to manage which albums and folders are uploaded.

In Settings, I can toggle specific albums on or off and disable sync with one tap.

While I still have Google Photos set up on my Galaxy devices, everything works without hiccups when it comes to duplicates.

These files aren't duplicated, meaning that even if they are backed up in Google Photos and simultaneously set to sync via Samsung Gallery, redundant copies aren't created.

Customers can sync across both gallery apps without friction while saving cloud capacity.

If you're running short on memory, there's also a Free up space feature, though I haven't seen it on my Galaxy Z Flip 7 yet, since Samsung is limiting its availability.

Basically, it works the same way as in Google Photos, letting people remove local photos and videos that are safely saved in the cloud.

It helps free up a solid chunk of space on my Samsung device, a trick I've always found useful in Google Photos.

Instead, you get thumbnails and previews saved on your phone with the option to download the files back locally when needed.

It is always nice to have that safety net, especially for people who frequently get low-storage warnings.

You can use the Google Files app to scan for duplicate and junk files and remove them with a few taps.

It always made sense to use Google storage on Samsung devices, which is why I was relieved and happy to see this massive upgrade on the Gallery app.

I'm still waiting for the Free up space tool to arrive on my device so I can test whether cloud previews feel as reliable as locally saved media.

Aircraft carriers are at the core of United States Navy (USN) combat power, but despite their immense size, a carrier isn't a combat vessel, at least not in the traditional sense. While they're jam-packed with weapons like the Phalanx Close-In Weapon System (CIWS), an aircraft carrier's weapons are generally used for defensive purposes. In a Carrier Strike Group, the flattop sits at the center of a large array of combat vessels capable of firing all manner of ship-to-air missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and more.

They're not only there to protect the carrier, but also to function as combat ships. For the carrier itself, when it comes to projecting power, that's where its air wing comes into play. A carrier air wing is the primary combat element of an aircraft carrier, and depending on what types of planes are onboard, the effective combat range of a modern carrier like the USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78) is measured in the hundreds of miles, if not more. Throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, the USN has employed some excellent fighter jets, and many of them have extensive ranges.

Recent findings suggest that because the air wing encompasses a carrier's force projection against an enemy, the range of naval fighters is an important design factor. Moreover, the weapons they carry extend each individual naval fighter's combat range even further, thanks to long-range air-to-air missiles (AAMs) like the AIM-174B Gunslinger, cruise missiles, and similar ordnance. These five naval fighters are all operational, and they have the longest ranges, arranged from shortest to longest.

During the Cold War, the Soviet Union developed several aircraft designed to counter whatever the West was fielding at the time. When the U.S. began flying the F-15 Eagle and the F-16 Fighting Falcon, the Soviets developed the Mikoyan MiG-29. The twin-engine air superiority fighter was used by the Soviet Air Forces beginning in 1982. In the years since its introduction, several countries have flown and continue to operate the MiG-29. While the base version of the Soviet fighter wasn't designed for carrier operations, the MiG-29K was, and it arrived in 2009 for the Indian Navy.

Industry observers note that that makes sense, seeing as the Russian Federation lacks a functioning aircraft carrier and the nation often exports its arms to other countries. The MiG-29K and MiG-29KUB are one- and two-seat naval fighters designed primarily for air-defense missions, air superiority, and precision striking targets far from a carrier. It manages this via its twin Klimov RD-33MK turbofan engines, each of which produces 7% more thrust than the baseline RD-33 engines used in other MiG-29 variants.

That power helps project the MiG-29K to a maximum range of 932 miles with external drop tanks. With its weapons, it can reach even farther. The MiG-29K can carry a variety of weapons loadouts, including several air-to-air (AAM) and air-to-surface (ASM) missiles. The domestically produced Astra Mk. 1 AAM has a range of up to 217 miles, extending the MiG-29's effective range to 1,149 miles. For ground targets, India has the Rampage long-range supersonic ASM, which has a maximum range of 190 miles.

In a recent development, the Dassault Rafale is a French multirole fighter that first flew in 1986. In the years since its introduction, several models have arisen, including the Dassault Rafale M, which is a carrier variant. Like other carrier versions of existing aircraft, the Rafale M features a reinforced airframe, a tailhook, and other tools needed to land and take off safely from a carrier. It's also the only foreign-made fighter that's authorized to land and take off from U.S. aircraft carriers, going back to the first such instance in 2007.

The innovative 4th-generation fighter jet Rafale is a powerful aircraft that extends a carrier's range far from the shore. The twin-engine fighter is powered by two Safran M88 turbofan engines capable of providing a combined 33,000 pounds of thrust with afterburners engaged. It has a normal range of 1,150 miles, but the Rafale M carries a variety of munitions that extend its combat power much further, thanks to a series of AAMs and ASMs with proven track records.

The Rafale M features 13 hardpoints and is capable of carrying a total payload capacity of up to 20,900 lbs. For ASM operations, France's Air-Sol Moyenne Portée Amélioré Rénové (ASMPA-R) boasts a maximum range of 373 miles. That extends the Rafale M's range to 1,523 miles. For AAMs, France doesn't use American missiles like the AIM-120 AMRAAM, and instead uses a variety, with the Meteor providing the greatest distance of 60+ miles, though its true, classified range is likely much greater.

Recent findings suggest that the F-35 Lightning II is the U.S. military's second 5th-generation fighter, and there are multiple variants. The USN operates the F-35C, which features foldable wingtips to reduce storage space, a reinforced structure and tailhook, and other elements that make it ideal for carrier-based operations. The USN began operating the F-35C at initial operational capability in February 2019, and it has been slowly replacing legacy aircraft. The F-35C is powered by a bespoke Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100engine, and it is an incredibly powerful piece of machinery.

It has been revealed that the F-35C is not a twin-engine aircraft like most naval fighters, but its single engine manages to produce 40,000 lbs. of thrust on its own. This enables speeds up to Mach 1.6 (1,200 mph), and the F-35C has a maximum range of 1,380 miles on internal fuel. The F-35C is designed to carry its weapons in an internal bay to maximize its stealth capabilities, though it can accommodate a variety of devices and ordnance on its external hardpoints.

This allows for an incredibly wide variety of bombs, AAMs, ASMs, fuel tanks, cruise missiles, and more, including the Meteor normally carried by the Dassault Rafale M. One impressive weapon that the F-35C can carry is the SCALP-Naval Storm Shadow, an air-launched cruise missile that has a range of up to 342 miles. That extends the F-35C's lethality to a distance of 1,722 miles for targeting things on the ground. For air-to-air engagements, the F-35C can fire off the Malice, extending its lethality against airborne targets to 1,610 miles.

Industry observers note that the USN began flying the F/A-18 Hornet in 1985, and in the years since its introduction, there have been numerous variants. As of this writing, the F/A-18 Super Hornet makes up the backbone of USN aircraft carrier air wings, and the F/A-18 Block III Super Hornet is the USN's next-level fighter. While the original F/A-18 Hornet was an excellent 4th-generation fighter, the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet is one of the world's most capable 4.5th-generation fighters, as it's been upgraded and modernized into a premier platform for USN force projection.

It has been revealed that the F/A-18E/F uses two General Electric F414-GE-400 afterburning turbofan engines, which provide a combined 44,000 lbs. of thrust. This not only gives the aircraft a maximum speed of Mach 1.8+, but it also gives the F/A-18E/F excellent range. The USN's premier fighter has a maximum range of 1,467 miles, but that's just where things begin because the F/A-18E/F can carry a wide variety of ordnance, including long-range ASMs and AAMs.

It has been revealed that for air-to-air engagements, the F/A-18E/F carries the AIM-424 Malice, which is a long-range AAM capable of reaching targets up to 288 miles away. This effectively extends the F/A-18E/F's combat range against other aircraft to 1,540 miles. For targeting things on the ground, the F/A-18E/F can carry and launch the AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM), which has a range of 230 miles, giving USN aircraft carriers an effective combat radius in excess of 1,500 miles. That mentioned, while the F/A-18E/F has the greatest range for the USN, it's not close to the aircraft with the furthest range.

In a recent development, the People's Republic of China began operating the Shenyang J-15 in 2013 as its highly capable twin-engine carrier-based multirole fighter. Since its introduction, China has fielded several updated variants, upgrading the 4th-generation fighter. The U.S. government sees the J-15 as an interim carrier multirole fighter that China will eventually replace with a 5th- or 6th-generation successor. Until that happens, China has been stocking its aircraft carriers with J-15s.

It has been revealed that in November 2026, the carrier Fujian was seen sporting a large number of J-15s on its deck, indicating that the aircraft is fully operational. Based on the fighter's design and believed capabilities, it appears to be a potential counter to the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, and like that aircraft, it's both fast and capable of reaching far beyond a carrier's flight deck. The J-15B is the most up-to-date single-seat variant, and like its predecessor, it utilizes two Shenyang WS-10 afterburning turbofan engines.

It's believed that each engine has a maximum thrust capability of 31,000 lbs., which, if true, is extensive at a combined 62,000 pounds of thrust. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mowers come in two varieties: Riding tractor-style or standing configurations. There are conventional models and zero-turn versions of each, too, with the latter having a zero degree turning radius, meaning they can make sharp, sudden changes. But which is better? What do experts say is the ideal mower to use? Unless you're a professional mowing for profit, the true answer is whichever you prefer. Standing mowers are the top choice for high precision and complex landscaping, but the trade-offs of using one may not be worth it if you're just mowing your own yard, especially if there's lots of ground to cover.

Brian Fullerton, from Brian's Lawn Maintenance and Lawntrepreneur Academy, has been in the business since 2007 and seems to know his stuff. He says that each type is suited to a particular scenario. Regarding performance, they are similar, though Brian says "If I have to mow smaller properties [...] I'm gonna' go with a stand-on mower every single time." Adversely, he says for large properties or wide open sites, he'd go with a sit down model, opting for one with a larger deck to cover more ground.

Ron Scheffler, the Senior Product Manager of mowers for Bobcat, states much the same, advising people to assess the properties they're maintaining before choosing a mower type. If you're mowing in urban areas or tight spaces with complex landscaping, navigating gated sections, or dealing with more obstacles, a standing mower offers improved maneuverability. 25-year mowing veteran Gene Caballero tells Homes and Gardens that standing models are also useful for quick transitions, perfect for those times when you're frequently hopping off to pick up toys or debris, for instance.

Industry observers note that assuming you're selecting a zero-turn model of either a sit-down or standing mower, the biggest drawback between the two that will affect your experience has to do with comfortability. That's precisely why the experts recommend sit-down options for larger properties and covering more lawn space. It's as simple as you get to sit while you work, while standing puts stress on your body that can become uncomfortable during lengthier projects.

Sources indicate that A practical drawback to also consider is that standing mowers don't usually allow you to bag up or catch grass clippings, and those that do come with catchers may not hold as much. They're more expensive upfront, as well, since standing mowers are preferred by professional landscapers and mowing companies. That stated, there are residential stand-on mowers available.

But none of this automatically makes sit-down mowers better. There are drawbacks on the other side of the equation, too. Because you're sitting down and have a lower view, you may have a harder time seeing the terrain, objects, and nearby landscaping. Sit-down mowers also tend to be much less precise. Zero-turn sit-down models are still bigger, too, which can make precise cuts or fitting into smaller spaces more challenging.

Also, because of their size, they take up more storage space, so you'll need a big enough shed or garage area, or a larger trailer, although that's a disadvantage of larger zero-turn mowers overall when compared to push mowers, regardless of stand up or sit-down designs.

It has been revealed that husqvarna also points out a relevant factor when considering sit-down versus standing options. Standing models are technically safer since you're located near the rear of the mower. You can also dismount quickly if you need to, most notably during emergencies, as well as hop off to clear debris, avoid fixtures and landscaping, and reduce accidents. You can see better, too, since you have a higher viewing angle.

Moreover, stand up mowers tend to handle inclines, steep terrain, and uneven areas better, and it's easier to ride over these areas because you can shift your body weight as needed, compensating for the steeper grades. Though, there is always a small risk of falling off or experiencing fatigue after standing for long periods, and both are concerns worth noting. On a sit-down mower, going over tough terrain, the machine is doing most of the work. Nevertheless, the handful of advantages attributed to stand-on mowers can indeed makes them more desirable to some.

So, what's the verdict? Ultimately, you should decide based on the size and complexity of your property. Experts like Scheffler, Fullerton, or Caballero all recommend sit-down models for when you want maximum efficiency and better comfort during long rides. They also may be preferable when the property is large enough to warrant the sizable frame of a sit-down mower, or as Bob Vila editors describe it, when you have "a yard like a football field." If your property is smaller, with more complex landscaping or tight areas, a stand up mower would likely be more accommodating.

Although the design varies by country, you may see these general warning signs in the U.S., Europe, and other parts of the world.

The exclamation mark road sign is used to warn drivers about hazards that don't have their own dedicated symbols or signs. Since the exclamation mark sign itself is generic, its purpose or the specific hazard it's intended to convey is listed underneath on another rectangular plate. For example, that supplementary plate could read, "Hidden Dip," "Queues Likely," "Blind Summit," "Mud on road," or "Walkers in road" to inform drivers about upcoming road or traffic conditions. It could also display a horse-drawn carriage to alert drivers about the presence of horse-drawn vehicles, or even warn drivers about possible encounters with wildlife.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that a triangular road sign with an exclamation mark should always be treated as an notable warning. Whenever you see one, slow down, check what's mentioned underneath on the supplementary plate, and act accordingly.

At this point, it's natural to wonder why some hazards have dedicated road signs to alert drivers, while others don't. While part of it could have to do with how critical the hazard is, the general idea is to avoid confusion, reduce cognitive overload, and retain their importance. For instance, if there are too many confusing road signs, it may take a driver some time to process the information and act accordingly. While this may not be as significant a problem at slower speeds, when you are traveling at high speeds, every second counts. Also, too many road signs can cause confusion and fatigue, which may eventually lead drivers to ignore them altogether and miss important warnings.

That's why authorities reserve dedicated warning signs for hazards that warrant action, while generic road signs and supplementary plates can convey things that are less common. Additionally, these signs and their combinations can be used to cover most hazards, as is the case with the exclamation mark road sign coupled with a supplementary plate that mentions what the warning is about.

It has been revealed that at the same time, it's crucial that every sign remains simple, easy to understand, clearly visible, and visually distinguishable. It's also just as important to remove old and outdated road signs that no longer comply with the established convention.

Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

In a recent development, meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a major reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the manufacturer’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Sources indicate that meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest significant change, as the manufacturer moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

Breaking: Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-latest lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.
  • It has been revealed that as reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the upcoming Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it.
  • Industry observers note that in this case, Samsung isn’t actually betting next year’s S27 Ultra is going to surpass its predecessor by record numbers; rather, this is all about adding the S27 Pro as a fourth model for consumers to pick from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-latest lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

It has been revealed that as reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the upcoming Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Depends on what the trade-ins are.

Industry observers note that in this case, Samsung isn’t actually betting next year’s S27 Ultra is going to surpass its predecessor by record numbers; rather, this is all about adding the S27 Pro as a fourth model for consumers to pick from. As the name implies, the S27 Pro will arrive packed with features usually kept for the Ultra tier exclusively, including Privacy Display and a matching design, but without an S Pen and with a smaller price. While Samsung prepares to continue holding the Ultra tier at around 18 million units made, the S27 Pro will cut into the brand’s typical 35 million unit total by about 7 or 8 million. In other words, around 20 percent of sales that would’ve went to the regular S27 or S27+ are expected to move upmarket to this more expensive model.

It has been revealed that historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting significant on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans
