⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter.
  • The search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the tech giant undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week.
  • Industry observers note that rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the company before leaving in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter. Haas is among several candidates under consideration, although it remains unclear whether he will get a formal offer and/or agree to take the position.

The search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the tech giant undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week. For now, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress serves as interim CEO. The company's board is right now searching for a permanent replacement and is reportedly evaluating both internal and external candidates. Neither Arm nor Nvidia commented on the matter to FT.

Industry observers note that rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the company before leaving in 2013. During his tenure as vice president at Nvidia, he was responsible for multiple projects, including notebook GPUs, Windows-on-Arm, and Tegra system-on-chips. Given that he held senior management positions, he certainly gained experience with Nvidia's operations, corporate culture, and relationships with customers and partners.

Sources indicate that furthermore, Haas has experience with the development of consumer and data center CPUs as well as GPUs and GPU IP, a combination that is hard to find in the industry. Haas reportedly maintains close ties with Jensen Huang and several members of Nvidia's board, which could make him a particularly attractive candidate for a company whose strategy and management structure have orbited around its founder for more than three decades.

While at Arm, Haas has demonstrated a willingness to make substantial strategic changes at the tech giant. Since Haas took the reins in 2022, Arm has introduced its Compute Subsystems (CSS) initiative, providing customers with complete and validated processor platform design, making it easier for newcomers to enter the market. Arm also introduced its first own-brand AGI CPU, putting the company in direct competition with some of its traditional customers. Both initiatives represent significant departures from Arm's traditional business model; however, they demonstrate Haas' readiness to pursue newly introduced revenue opportunities despite risks and the possibility of damaging relationships with long-term partners.

Sources indicate that another advantage is Haas' extensive experience with the semiconductor industry in general. Arm's CPU and GPU technologies are used in system-on-chips developed by hundreds of companies that have very distinctive requirements, including Nvidia itself, Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek, just to name a few.

According to recent reports, in addition, Haas led Arm through its initial public offering in 2023 and therefore has experience with investors and regulators. Also, Haas happens to be the CEO of SoftBank, the parent of Arm.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Nevertheless, Haas' potential appointment would not be without challenges, primarily because he has never managed a firm the scale of Nvidia. Arm has around 10,000 employees worldwide; it develops and licenses various semiconductor IP, primarily CPU and GPU technologies, to a wide range of customers with distinct needs. By contrast, Nvidia designs CPUs, GPUs, networking equipment, complete AI systems, and software platforms and has a headcount of about 42,000. As a result, if Haas becomes the boss of Nvidia, he will have to manage a considerably bigger organization with a dramatically more complicated product portfolio and supply chain. Furthermore, replacing Huang, who has led Nvidia since its establishment in 1993 and personally shaped its technology strategy and business tactics, would be a formidable task for virtually any executive.

Ironically, Haas' appointment (if it happens) would create an unusual situation in which Nvidia will be led by the chief executive of a tech giant it attempted to acquire in 2020 and abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid regulatory opposition.

#312. Latest Update: Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Latest Update: Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.
  • The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.
  • AMD also revealed that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.

The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.

AMD also revealed that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.

Google's April 2026 launch split its eighth generation hardware into the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference. Google bills this as the first time it has introduced four TPU systems in one year, but as ServeTheHome points out, the two newcomers are system configurations built on existing chips rather than new designs.

As per Taiwanese outlet INSIDE, the 8tx inherits the 8t's 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of HBM, but swaps in the lower-latency Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty, and pitches the system at regulated enterprises and governments that want to fine-tune, distill, and train agents on private data without moving it between clusters.

According to recent reports, AMD notes Epyc handles orchestration, data preparation, and the high-throughput link to the accelerators. Its Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) works with the TPU to extend the protected environment out to the accelerators, checking each one's identity and security configuration before granting direct access to protected memory.

Industry observers note that prompts, model weights, and intermediate data stay encrypted in host memory and in transit, according to AMD, with hardware isolation while the TPU runs. Google, for its part, described the result as "keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use.".

Recent findings suggest that google hasn't directly remarked why it passed over Axion, the Neoverse V2-based chip it unveiled in 2024 as its first data center processor. Its own documentation offers a strong hint, however: Google's list of supported Confidential VM configurations runs entirely on AMD SEV and Intel TDX machines, with no Axion-based C4A or N4A instances, and states that TPUs can't right now be attached to Confidential VMs at all.

AMD's release adds that Google security experts have performed deep reviews of AMD's security processor firmware, and that SEV already underpins Google's Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow services.

It could be argued here that confidential computing is only as credible as the years spent attacking it, and Google's audited chain of trust runs through x86. Building an equivalent on Axion would mean qualifying new hardware before shipping a product whose entire selling point is the "trust" it comes with, making it a moot point.

The move however is not a win for AMD's latest silicon; ServeTheHome reported that Google chose Turin to match the TPU 8t's PCIe Gen5 x16 interface, noting that a Gen6 host such as Venice would add no accelerator bandwidth, and tying the decision to Google's 2027 qualification schedule. Venice is AMD's 2nm flagship; the 8tx runs on a chip based on a family of CPUs that introduced in October 2024.

Mark Lohmeyer, who runs AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, told reporters that select customers will be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers, Data Center Knowledge reported, noting that Oracle recently remarked it will offer TPUs on its cloud. INSIDE quoted Lohmeyer arguing that the technology lowers the risk of physical operators reaching sensitive data, even in third-party facilities.

It has been revealed that as TPUs spread beyond Google's own campuses, hardware attestation becomes the mechanism that lets a model owner place weights on hardware someone else runs. That interestingly puts AMD as a crucial part at the root of Google's off-campus trust offerings, a bigger role than the 8tx's niche positioning would initially suggest.

According to recent reports, it also revives August's rumor: A SemiAnalysis client note reported by Tom's Hardware, noted "Market chatter suggests [Google] is working with AMD on a TPU project in the v10 generation," possibly with CPU cores on the same package. The 8tx confirms neither claim as its Epyc chips sit in separate sockets, and nothing announced on November 9 involves AMD in accelerator design, but it does lend credence to potential future collaborations between the chip designer and the AI juggernaut.

The news saw AMD closing at $508.58 on November 9, up 13.26%, after trading as high as $515.18 on more than twice its recent average volume and while not all of it can be attributed to this particular development even as Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer upgraded AMD to Outperform with a $600 target, calling its server and data center success "undeniable", one could argue that it was a sizeable, if not the overwhelming catalyst in play that day.

The TPU 8tx arguably won't turn AMD's Epyc into a formidable TPU business overnight, and Google has left enough unpublished that its confidential computing claims deserve scrutiny once customers can test them.

However, one does need to account for the fact that when Google needed a host CPU to stake its first confidential TPU on, it picked AMD over its own chip, and that endorsement will outlast one day's share price increase as the latter aims to broaden its AI business even as its CEO recently branded the tech giant as "Data center-first" entity even as PC sales continue to plummet.

#310. Tech Report: Nearly 20 years after launch, ancient AMD Radeon HD 2000 and 3000 GPUs finally get a Linux fix for corrupted video playback

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (749 w)
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Tech Report: Nearly 20 years after launch, ancient AMD Radeon HD 2000 and 3000 GPUs finally get a Linux fix for corrupted video playback

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves.
  • Recent findings suggest that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8).
  • Interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves. As spotted by Phoronix, the fix targets the Unified Video Decoder (UVD) engine across the RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635, and RV670 silicon families, making up the Radeon HD 2000 and HD 3000 families released starting in 2007. Linux people running these cards experienced visual corruption during hardware-accelerated video playback whenever the GPU was simultaneously handling active 3D or desktop drawing workloads; those challenges should now be resolved.

Recent findings suggest that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8). When the decoder was reading compressed video from system memory while the GPU was drawing, it would corrupt video frames. Moving the input to VRAM allowed frames to decode correctly. Disabling graphics draws also stopped the corruption. Here is a proposal to keep UVD buffers in VRAM for this family of devices, as the driver already does for some other chips. The patch covers RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635 and RV670. These chips share the RV6xx decoder path and legacy R600 firmware, so I think they are likely to have the same hardware requirements. Someone with the other hardware would need to verify that. I tested this on Debian. I used Codex to help with the investigation, testing and patch.

Interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path. The culprit turned out to be a memory placement oversight: the driver wasn't consistently keeping UVD input buffers pinned inside dedicated VRAM. When graphics draw calls competed for resources, frames failed to decode properly. By forcing those buffers to stay in VRAM — a behavior the Radeon kernel driver apparently already enforced for several other chip families — video playback cleans right up.

Industry observers note that it is easy to forget just how pivotal the R600 generation was for PC graphics. Launching in 2007 as the first desktop GPU lineup built under the AMD banner following that firm's blockbuster acquisition of the Canadian ATI Technologies Inc., the Radeon HD 2000 series marked the latest AMD graphics division's transition away from separate pixel and vertex pipelines on the desktop, after implementing the tech first for the Xbox 360. The move to a unified shader architecture arrived alongside DirectX 10 and Windows Vista, so it was a time of many transitions.

While the flagship Radeon HD 2900 XT famously struggled against Nvidia's dominant GeForce 8800 GTX in raw gaming rasterization and power draw, the R600 family brought serious multimedia chops to the table. The introduction of the first-generation Unified Video Decoder (UVD) on the mainstream RV610 and RV630 chips, and later the refined RV670 powering the beloved Radeon HD 3850 and 3870, allowed even budget PCs to offload heavy H.264 and VC-1 Blu-ray decoding from the CPU. In 2007, smooth 1080p playback without maxing out a dual-core processor was a major selling point for many users, but none more so than home theater PC (HTPC) builders.

It has been revealed that of course, almost nobody is daily driving a TeraScale 1 graphics card in 2026, especially when modern integrated graphics run circles around them at a fraction of the wattage; the contributor who submitted the patches wants them for his ancient Core 2 Duo-based iMac. Yet, there is something quietly heartwarming about the longevity of open-source Linux drivers. Whereas proprietary Windows support for the HD 2000 and 3000 series was sunsetted over a decade ago, the mainline Linux kernel continues to carry the torch. Combined with recent AI-assisted cleanup efforts across the Mesa R600 user-space driver, vintage Radeon hardware is arguably in better software shape today than it was during its actual retail lifespan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience.

Recent findings suggest that but even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

According to recent reports, unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without matter. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

It does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

Because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

According to recent reports, the Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

Industry observers note that on the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

It has been revealed that I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It has been revealed that it uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only issue I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

It has been revealed that the homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

Industry observers note that the buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

In a recent development, it’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

In a recent development, as far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained how they tried to modernize the Bond franchise while retaining its classic roots.
  • In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Henson and Smith discussed their inspirations for the game's soundtrack and revealed that their primary goal was to push the franchise into a more contemporary direction while keeping the familiar elements fans love.
  • "Luckily there is a huge catalogue of music, film and novels to dive into, and we took inspiration from all of them, as well as other sources not in the Bond world," Henson mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained how they tried to modernize the Bond franchise while retaining its classic roots.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Henson and Smith discussed their inspirations for the game's soundtrack and revealed that their primary goal was to push the franchise into a more contemporary direction while keeping the familiar elements fans love.

"Luckily there is a huge catalogue of music, film and novels to dive into, and we took inspiration from all of them, as well as other sources not in the Bond world," Henson mentioned. "Our mission we set ourselves was to give the franchise a gentle nudge into the modern day, without completely reinventing it. It was always going to sound like James Bond.".

Smith added that he loves the original Ian Fleming novels and used First Light "as an excuse to re-read them on the train into work each day.".

It has been revealed that "But like we said before, one of the great things about this franchise is its ability to stay current and adapt," he said. "So, the possibility of going some different places with the music was always there.".

While the pair's catalogue of inspiration was "huge" and offered plenty of references, Henson confessed that they tried not to look too much at the previous Bond games, but "we took the time to watch the film series to study the scores in a different light, now that we knew we’d be working on our own.".

"So many great composers have added their voice to the franchise, from John Barry to Eric Serra, Michael Kamen to Hans Zimmer, and it is fascinating to hear how each one approaches the material," the composer said.

Smith added, "That made it easier, actually. The fact that the music has gone in so many different directions already made us more confident to pursue our own.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO.
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers.
  • Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Sources indicate that turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

There are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

#304. Today I learned why wind farms paint one turbine blade black

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (653 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Techradar

Today I learned why wind farms paint one turbine blade black

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you'd think that painting a single turbine blade black is a pretty inexpensive fix for accidental bird deaths.
  • Industry observers note that at the Smøla wind farm in Norway, every wind turbine had one of its blade painted black for an extended science experiment back in August 2013.
  • However, similar experiments in the Netherlands did not yield positive results, because apparently this fix depends heavily on the local bird species and population size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you'd think that painting a single turbine blade black is a pretty inexpensive fix for accidental bird deaths. It sounds almost too good to be true, which perhaps it is.

Industry observers note that at the Smøla wind farm in Norway, every wind turbine had one of its blade painted black for an extended science experiment back in August 2013. Over the next three years, the number of bird carcasses found fell by 70%.

However, similar experiments in the Netherlands did not yield positive results, because apparently this fix depends heavily on the local bird species and population size.

In a recent development, there are a total of 68 turbines at the Smøla wind power plant, an archipelago off the coast of Central Norway. Researchers from the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research compared four regular turbines with four neighboring ones that had one blade painted black for this experiment.

They regularly counted the number of bird carcasses within 100 meters of the wind farm. This continued over a period of more than ten years, combining 7.5 years of baseline data from before painting any turbine blades to 3.5 years of data from after. In 2020, they published their findings in a paper called Ecology and Evolution.

In a recent development, turns out that this small change in visual cues reduced the number of bird deaths by over 70%, proving especially effective on the somewhat rare white-tailed sea eagle population of the region. While the researchers noted that this anecdotal data may not hold up to different bird populations, this was still independent real-world confirmation of a separate laboratory experiment that found similar results in 2003.

What difference does one black blade make? According to researchers, it has to do with how birds process visual cues.

In a recent development, animation designers call it motion smearing, where images that move too fast for the human eye to follow are inferred in the brain as one continuous motion. When turbine blades are in motion, birds find it difficult to notice the threat because the unicolor rotating blades look like one giant circle.

Sources indicate that when you paint one of these blades black, it breaks up the pattern so the moving blades are more easily distinguishable to the eye. But as Audubon reported, these are preliminary findings that won't translate to all bird species equally — especially ones that don't have the visual acuity to notice the difference. There's also a significant amount of effort involved, since painting turbines in operation requires both lifts and specialist crews who can navigate the height.

Most of the land experiments so far have stuck with black, but at sea, a latest trial is experimenting with a different color.

In a recent development, dutch consortium Ecowende is fitting seven Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines with one red 115.5-meter blade each. Red was chosen after weighing options against criteria such as durability and heat management, apart from the obvious benefit of being more easily discernible from a distance.

In a recent development, that remarked, seabirds may generally need less help than expected. A Vattenfall and Spoor study at its Aberdeen offshore wind farm tracked 2,007 flight paths over 19 months. It found no confirmed collisions, with birds typically keeping 100 to 200 meters away.

  • In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer also reacted to BioWare's closure, Wall shared what it was like creating a sci-fi RPG score with Sam Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates.
  • In a recent development, "This was the game that helped me understand the value, importance, and just how much fun and rewarding collaborating with other composers can be," Wall remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Original Mass Effect composer Jack Wall has recalled working on BioWare's role-playing game (RPG), describing the collaborative project as a "rewarding" experience that reminded him of how important it is to work with other composers.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer also reacted to BioWare's closure, Wall shared what it was like creating a sci-fi RPG score with Sam Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates.

In a recent development, "This was the game that helped me understand the value, importance, and just how much fun and rewarding collaborating with other composers can be," Wall remarked. "I’m a decent enough composer, but I feel my real strength is in storytelling and making sure the production and music serve the story and guiding a team to that goal.".

The composer, who also shared how orchestral and synth music influenced the first two games, explained that working with other composers helped the project in the long run, despite his own talents, saying, "It’s sometimes easier to work with other composers to help you fulfill the mandate of having music be this unseen character in the game that really tells the story sonically and helps the player be more immersed in the experience.".

Recent findings suggest that wall added, "You can suddenly float to the 30,000-foot level and understand how it’s all supposed to work together. Not that you can’t do that on your own, but it’s just easier, more fluid, and you get there in sort of a 1 + 1 = 3 way.

"I like that insta-grat [instant gratification] of having the music finished sooner so you can really play with it and hone it.".

Elsewhere, Wall also shared his stance on artificial intelligence being used as a replacement in video games, saying, "AI is not an artist.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment.
  • Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Chinese military medical school has just developed a UAV that could remotely administer medicine, helping treat injured soldiers on the front lines without putting medical personnel at risk. According to Chinese mouthpiece Global Times, the Air Force Medical University built the first casualty-search drone for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that fires darts loaded with painkillers to help ease the pain of wounded personnel.

“We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment. For example, we can use drones to inject medication into wounded personnel from a considerable distance,” Air Force Medical University representative Wang Jianqi told the publication. “Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle, buying valuable time for treatment.”.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions. However, the four-year escalation of the 12-year war has seen the creative implementations of these units — from jam-proof fiber optic drones to the use of heavy-lift hexacopters for medical evacuation. Now, drones-as-first-responders are being developed for civilian use, including firefighting drones, camera response drones, and even “Campus Guardian Angel” drones designed to neutralize school shooters.

However, China's air-ground treatment drone remains in the experimental stage, says Wang. After all, you can’t just administer medication without assessing the patient’s vital signs and their injuries. It’s also difficult or even impossible to load an incapacitated soldier without external assistance. Still, the deployment of medical UAVs would help with battlefield medicine, which has developed the concept of the “golden hour,” which suggests that wounded personnel treated within the first hour have the greatest chance of survival.

Recent findings suggest that although battlefield medicine was in use since the 1800s, especially during Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and the American Civil War, helicopter medevacs were first deployed during World War 2 in Burma and the Philippines. The Korean War saw the introduction of MASH — Mobile Army Surgical Hospital — units that brought forward treatment units closer to the frontline.

This, combined with the widespread use of UH-1 Hueys during the Vietnam War to evacuate wounded soldiers from the front lines, sometimes while under enemy fire, has greatly increased the survival rate among wounded soldiers. Today, helicopter and ground medevacs are common among military forces, with drone treatment and evacuation now being experimented with in both the frontlines of Ukraine and military medical universities in China.

According to recent reports, doom’s iconic anti-hero is ripping and tearing his way into Rainbow Six Siege. Heading to the game on December 22, players will get a chance to rip and tear their way across the Siege universe as part of the game’s long-awaited fourth season. According to recent reports, the Doom Slayer skin comes after a wave of recent similar collaborations, with everything from Halo, Resident Evil, and Tomb Raider skins making appearances in Ubisoft’s FPS. “Doom means so much to me personally, and for many on the team that played Doom as kids growing up,” notes Game Director Chris Budgens. “I think that skins are the best way [to implement most collaborations]. With skins, we get a lot more leeway in terms of having fun with the characters and franchises.

To date, Rainbow Six Siege has only one permanent canon playable operator from a different fictional universe — Metal Gear Solid’s Solid Snake — and as The Doom Slayer joins as a skin, it appears that Ubisoft Montreal wants to keep it that way for now. “We don't want to just flood the game with different partners,” reflects Budgens. “It has to be right.”.

In a recent development, snake’s inclusion, it seems, has been well judged. Since Solid Snake’s surprise introduction to Siege in March 2026, he’s become a beloved character in the game, slotting into Siege’s more grounded fictional universe with surprising ease. As I sit backstage at the Osaka 2026 majors, Ubisoft Montreal tells me that Solid Snake’s inclusion was an IP infiltration years in the making. “We had originally brought up the idea, and [Konami] were interested right from the get-go,” reveals Budgens. “One of the funny things was, what does this actually look like? Are we going with a skin? We had some interest in bringing Solid Snake as the operator into the game, but we had never really done that before—an operator from another franchise.”.

Creative director Joshua Mills, however, needed a bit more convincing that Snake would work in Siege’s gritty, grounded universe. “Alex Karpazis, the previous creative director, brought the idea to me and said, 'Listen, I want to bring [Snake] into the game, and I was like, 'You want to do what? How's that going to work?'” recalls Mills, “'If you say the cardboard box, I'm walking away right now!”.

Sources indicate that in order to make Snake work alongside Sam Fisher and alongside SWAT team-esque operators, they decided to reimagine Snake as a Tom Clancy-esque agent. “We came up with a very clear rationale, which was: it's Solid Snake as if he existed within the Rainbow Six universe,” recalls Mills. “It allows us to take everything that's iconic about the character and make it more grounded and canon in Rainbow Six…. Then we got to make that legendary pairing with Snake and Zero [Sam Fisher], an opportunity of a lifetime to be able to do that.”.

In a recent development, where the Doom Slayer is very much a classic skin-based collaboration, Mills suggests that The Boss’ inclusion in Rainbow Six Siege has opened the door to future fully fledged third-party operators. “We've definitely talked about other collaborations for a canon-based operator,” teases Mills. "We're very, very strict about who we would work with on this and who we would bring in because, again, we have to rationalise it one way or another. You can't just take any IP character and throw them in because it just doesn't work. That's where skin collaborations work fine… [but for operators ] There are some ideas, but nothing to confirm at the moment.".

#297. Lawyer’s eight-V100 AI server moves DeepSeek from 2-bit to near-NVFP4 precision

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1354 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Lawyer’s eight-V100 AI server moves DeepSeek from 2-bit to near-NVFP4 precision

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an upgrade, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090.
  • Once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity.
  • In a recent development, he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an upgrade, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the upcoming build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.

Once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.

In a recent development, he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he indicates it’s not as good as frontier.

He reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.

The original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his company’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README claims that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the newly introduced build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.

The workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.

Industry observers note that measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.

In a recent development, this does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the new two-request setup he now runs.

Recent findings suggest that the result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.

Recent findings suggest that each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.

Sources indicate that builder’s measurements, Nov. 5 (2-bit) and Nov. 12 (near-NVFP4); greedy decoding, thinking off, one request at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.

As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.

He also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The strategy is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you tuned in to the Rainbow Six Siege Osaka majors this weekend, you’ll have noticed that a long-sidelined operator took center stage — Doc.
  • Industry observers note that A pre-Finals panel revealed that in Season 4, the largely forgotten healing character will be getting a huge revamp.
  • It turns out, it's a good time to be a support player, because the Doc isn't the only healer-focused upgrade coming next season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you tuned in to the Rainbow Six Siege Osaka majors this weekend, you’ll have noticed that a long-sidelined operator took center stage — Doc. As 20 teams duked it out in front of a screaming crowd, competing to earn $200,000 in prize money, the trophy they were coveting was shaped in the likeness of the healer-focused operator. As palpable tension rippled through the packed ATC hall, moments before the tournament’s final, we soon discovered why.

Industry observers note that A pre-Finals panel revealed that in Season 4, the largely forgotten healing character will be getting a huge revamp. Instead of shooting direct stim pistol darts from afar, Doc will now be armed with a brand new gadget — the E-HEAL Monitor system. Using the E-HEAL, Doc will be able to remotely heal and — even revive — teammates from across the map (including through walls).

It turns out, it's a good time to be a support player, because the Doc isn't the only healer-focused upgrade coming next season. Operator Thunderbird is also coming back in a big way, with her Kóna Stations receiving a significant buff. Her number of Kóna Stations will be increased from 3 to 4 for broader site coverage, and if that wasn't enough to make you consider her, she’ll receive a newly introduced weapon too: the MBZ-19. Thunderbirds really are go.

Alongside these intriguing operator remasters, an FPS legend is joining the fray — the Doom Slayer. In this surprise collaboration with Doom, the iconic anti-hero will become a part of Siege on December 22 in skin form — and you can read more about that here.

Sources indicate that the beloved map Bank has also had an revision that seeks to level the playing field between attackers and defenders. Adding a new access point and exterior cover around the entry point, Ubisoft Montreal claims they're aiming to rebalance a map that's currently weighted too heavily in the defenders' favour. A new temporary testing ground will also allow the community to weigh in on a potential new secondary gadget which allows defenders to reinforce just part of a wall, leaving the rest open for lines of sight.

Sources indicate that yet for hardcore fans, some of the most welcome changes will be the least exciting on paper. For year 11 and season 4, Rainbow Six Siege's UI has undergone a drastic overhaul, and with it, new types of matchmaking have been introduced.

The Ranked ecosystem is getting an overhaul, splitting the competitive mode into dedicated Ranked Solo/Duo and Ranked Flex playlists. The aim is to keep individual and duo players from clashing with larger, coordinated squads, hopefully saving some frustration and heartache for solo players. This will work in conjunction with Cross-Queue Matchmaking, in a bid to keep those match queue times fast. Additionally, the level requirement to unlock Ranked will be dropping from 50 to 30, helping newer players to jump in sooner.

“The solo/duo ranked playlist is something that we've been trying to do for years,” beams Rainbow Six Siege Game Director Chris Budgens, "We've always gotten cold feet, so we started looking at how we actually pull off a solo queue within Siege, while respecting healthy queue times and so on. Every time we tried to do it, we would get scared by the data — this might be a bit more destructive than we're ready to deal with at the moment because we had other known quantities such as Rank 3.0 we wanted to work on.”.

“We had so much data support in terms of our analysts and simulations and matchmaking queue times, and finally cracked it,” he adds. “We're really happy to be able to bring that to players because they've been asking for years to have a solo queue playlist.”.

Alongside new ranking queues, playing with your friends promises to be markedly less of a pain in the backside. An all-new Social Hub consolidates Ubisoft Connect and first-party platform friends into a single list, aiming to offer cleaner and less intrusive notifications. Players will now be able to invite friends to games via a single code, letting you generate a squad code to share on social media, negating the need to search for them on Ubisoft Connect.

According to recent reports, alongside the newly introduced invite system, the store’s been overhauled, aiming to provide clearer — and easier — browsing. Celebration packs will be making a return via the Winter Daily Rewards. Out of every 20 Winter Daily Rewards, five will be celebration packs. There’s now also finally a way to open multiple packs at once, letting players tear into multiple Alpha/Event packs at once to promptly clear out their pack log. While not a reveal that will get fans pumping the air in excitement, it all adds up to a smoother play experience, which is a welcome change in our book.

It has been revealed that all in all, Season 4 looks to add a series of welcome — but not groundbreaking — improvements to Rainbow Six Siege. Yet while Season 4 so far may lack the excitement of a Solid Snake announcement, it points to a wider confidence in Siege — careful iteration rather than a table-up ending, solidifying the game's foundations before any potentially misguided attempts at innovation.

“One of the core vision steps we're looking at is protecting and focusing on excellence across the game in a lot of different ways — improving all the different things we do,” reflects Creative Director Joshua athan Mills on Season 4 and Ubisoft Montreal’s vision for continuing to shape Siege, “Whether that be anti-cheat, serviceability, or all sorts of things like this, we want to hone it and perfect it because 10 years in, Siege knows what it is, and it's important to listen to it and drive that forward.”.

#294. Sennheiser keeps the Momentum going with great improvements over the True Wireless 4

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1525 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidcentral

Sennheiser keeps the Momentum going with great improvements over the True Wireless 4

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a lot to talk about with the Momentum True Wireless 5, because they're an upgrade compared to the Momentum TW 4 in almost every way that matters.
  • Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Sennheiser is one of my go-to audio brands for quality consumer and reference audio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a lot to talk about with the Momentum True Wireless 5, because they're an upgrade compared to the Momentum TW 4 in almost every way that matters. From sound quality to ANC and quality-of-life improvements, if you prioritize sound over ANC, Sennheiser’s latest is worth serious consideration.

Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Sennheiser is one of my go-to audio brands for quality consumer and reference audio. And for good reason: they often produce products that have crystal clarity, are well-balanced with great detail retrieval, while still being fun to listen to rather than clinical.

When it comes to their Bluetooth devices, they prioritize audio quality over active noise canceling, but with the introduction of their new Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5, they’re closer than ever to ANC market leaders Sony and Bose.

Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5.

Bluetooth 6.0, Multipoint support.

7 mm TrueResponse dynamic drivers.

SBC, AAC, aptX Adaptive, aptX Lossless (Snapdragon Sound).

Up to 6 hours (ANC on), 20-25 total with charging case; User-replaceable batteries.

USB-C, 2 hrs for full charge; 8 min charging for up to 1 hr playtime.

8-band EQ (app), Personalized sound.

6 mics combined with 2 bone-conduction voice accelerometers.

Copper, Cream, Graphite, Denim, Lavender.

While I love Sennheiser’s sound quality, their boxy Bluetooth earbuds have not been the stuff of aesthetic excellence.

I’ve never called previous models “ugly,” but their looks have been rather dull. The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 (Momentum TW5 from here on) look like an artisan took the TW4 and carved away the boxy shape, smoothing those angular edges into a sleek, aerodynamic aesthetic (see the photo comparison in the gallery above).

This year, I have the Copper colorway, which is a combination of beautiful copper earbuds and case trim with textured brown case exteriors and the signature Sennheiser logo in copper on the ‘buds and silver on the case top. The case fits much better in my pants’ coin pocket this year than last year. Gone is the small, boxy case. Instead, you get a slim, pocketable case with wired and wireless charging, plus other features I’ll touch on shortly.

The earbuds from the previous generation fit my ears well, thanks to their shape and the silicone wings around the edges. The wings are gone now, but with the newly introduced shape and ergonomics, they fit my ears just as well as they did before, and that’s despite actually being heavier than the Momentum TW4, which also feels bulkier in my ears compared to the new Momentum TW5.

Though the aesthetic upgrade is definitely welcome, the most important upgrades for many people will likely be the audio improvements in both sound reproduction and active noise canceling.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Let’s talk ANC, first. During my day one testing, I realized I’d need to pull out my previously tested Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds because my first listen had me wondering whether Sennheiser had upped their ANC game to those levels; it was that good!

Sources indicate that when it comes to noise-canceling earbuds, you can focus on either sound quality or aggressive noise canceling. Prioritizing one often comes at the expense of the other, so while Sennheiser’s ANC on previous models was good, it wasn’t market-leading. This time, Sennheiser’s engineers have greatly improved ANC across the frequency spectrum.

Industry observers note that though I wouldn’t run out to upgrade my earbuds just for improved ANC, this year’s model is definitely more aggressive at canceling noise than the Momentum TW4. You’ll hear more complete cancellation across the frequency spectrum. That means that you’ll hear less high-pitched urban traffic noise or subway sounds. Keyboard keystrokes should be a bit quieter. Cars whizzing by you; their engine noises will have decreased compared to the previous generation.

It has been revealed that and while that's true when you compare the Momentum TW5 to the TW4, Sony’s WF-1000XM6 still hushes more of those same frequencies than the TW5. The difference in 2026 is that Sennheiser has closed the distance between the ANC it offers and what you’ll get from Sony.

While the durability hasn’t changed, the Momentum TW5 carries the same IP54 rating as the previous generation; Sennheiser has upgraded the longevity of this year’s model with user-replaceable batteries in both the earbuds and the charging case.

Sources indicate that on the charging case, that upgrade is pretty clear if you look at the single Philips head screw on the bottom right side of the case, across from the oddly placed USB-C charging port on the left. I’m guessing that port placement is the result of making the battery removable.

Sources indicate that the Momentum TW5 comes with a prying tool to remove the battery, but you’ll need to provide the Philips PH000 screwdriver. This is a Phillips head (the “star”) screwdriver with a 7mm blade. Sennheiser lists the battery part number as BA 501, but it isn’t listed for sale on their site yet.

I thoroughly enjoy Sennheiser’s sound signature. I use their IE900 IEMs as reference in-ear headphones, and their HD660S as one of my over-ear reference audio headphones, along with pairs from Dali and Fosi. The Momentum TW5 expands sound quality across the frequency range, with its signature focus on the mid-range to deliver great instrument separation and strong vocal presentation without sacrificing low-end energy.

It has been revealed that listening to Charles Mingus’ “Moanin’,” the TW5 does a much better job than the Sony WF-1000XM6 at maintaining a strong sense of instrumentation during the song's most frenetic parts. Where Sony turns those sections into a pot of mashed potatoes, Sennheiser allows you to continue to hear where the sound of different instruments comes from in the stereo image.

Listening to various folk songs, including Paul Simon’s “Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes,” where his voice can get sibilant with audio products that have harsher, or overly energetic high-frequency reproduction, the TW5 were smooth. No sibilance from Simon, and no eardrum-fatiguing high notes from Joni Mitchell’s “River (With French Horns) [Blue Sessions].”.

Around the minute mark on Mitchell’s song, she hits some sustained high notes that drive me batty on clinical headphones or those with poor high-frequency reproduction, but again, the TW5 are more on the smooth end of the spectrum.

If you listen and disagree with my assessment, the good news is that this year the Sennheiser Smart Control+ app has expanded its five-band EQ to eight bands, so you’ll have more control over shaping the sound to your preferences, and the pair of buds take well to EQ adjustments.

My only real issue with the TW5 was the microphones when making phone calls. They sound excellent indoors, but outdoors, they'll block noise superbly, but at the cost of audio stability. At times, when the AI is working hard to block background noise, I've found that audio quality can take a hit. Overall, you'll sound great, and so will the folks calling you, but be aware that, depending on ambient noise, you may experience some finicky behavior.

In terms of battery life, I've found that I can get a day's use out of them with ANC off. For me, that's around 10 hours, including a trip to my local climbing gym. ANC on has given less, though a little better than some competitors, getting a little over six hours in my testing. More bass-heavy tracks in your rotation will affect that, though.

In the final analysis, you have Bluetooth earbuds that folks love for various reasons. Some lock you into an ecosystem and are superior in part because of how they work inside that walled garden, while others are more open and fully stand on their own.

The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are the latter, and while they aren’t market leaders in ANC or calling, they’re solid performers in those areas and offer a delightfully entertaining, engaging sound signature that you’ll get extra years out of, thanks to their user-serviceable batteries.

Industry observers note that sennheiser gives consumers a worthy upgrade over the Momentum True Wireless 5. They've improved the sound and noise-cancelling quality, made the batteries removable in both the buds and the case, and refined the exterior. A worthy upgrade!

#290. Breaking: Weeks after shipment was swiped by China, Pentagon ‘struggles to account for’ $31 billion in missing F-35 aircraft parts

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (533 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Breaking: Weeks after shipment was swiped by China, Pentagon ‘struggles to account for’ $31 billion in missing F-35 aircraft parts

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week.
  • Inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source.
  • Chief among the challenges that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week. In its report — published just weeks after China purportedly swiped a classified shipment of F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong — the GAO criticized the current inventory system as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.” Possible solutions were also provided by the GAO; however, the implications are that the most advanced and costly fighter jets in U.S. history may not be ready and reliable due to inventory management deficiencies.

Inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source. The F-35 program is estimated to cost $1.9 trillion over its lifecycle. It is the most costly weapon system in history, indicates the GAO. But the Department of Defense (DOD) has “long-standing and ongoing deficiencies related to the accountability and financial reporting of F-35 parts,” asserts the watchdog.

Chief among the challenges that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts. These are spread among 700 government and contractor facilities worldwide, but the technology for managing massive inventories has existed for decades.

We might have seen a telling symptom of the inadequate F-35 parts tracking system back in September. A communications and/or accountability breakdown resulted in a UPS worker routing top-secret parts through Hong Kong to save time. They were allegedly swiped by China after an employee is thought to have missed an email warning not to divert the parts.

Frustratingly, this is the third report since 2019 from the GAO, and the latest published report complains that the DOD has “made minimal progress” in implementing past recommendations. For example, in a 2022 report, periodic physical inventories of F-35 parts were recommended but have not been implemented yet, notes Stars and Stripes. There is also no reliable procedure for verifying data from prime contractors, which can be “inaccurate and incomplete.”.

Presently, it is believed that there are over 1 million parts, worth more than $85 million, that are lost or missing. Moreover, about 17,000 parts that have been sent in for repair, worth as much as $42.5 billion, aren’t tracked.

According to recent reports, stars and Stripes mentions that the Pentagon is working on “a live connection” for the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO), bridging its inventory software and that of prime contractors with F-35 parts. The JPO asserts that it is now modernizing its infrastructure with direct real-time interfaces. “This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” remarked a JPO spokesperson, quoted by Breaking Defense.

If there are multiple devices that match a command, Gemini can now ask a quick follow-up question to determine exactly which device you mean instead of guessing or giving up. Sources indicate that google is also offering Nest Hub owners a more useful way to interact with Gemini. The Google Home app enhancement fixes a number of camera problems, especially for older Nest hardware that has been moved to the newer app. Google has fixed some live-streaming connection challenges with the first-generation Nest Cam Indoor, Nest Cam Outdoor, wired Nest Doorbell (Nest Hello), and both Nest Cam IQ models.

The fixes target particular network setups like PPPoE connections, fiber internet, and mobile hotspots. Nest Cam IQ owners should also get back event thumbnails, and improved clock accuracy should provide more reliable timestamps on recorded footage. Google also updated security certificates and fixed stability issues that could lead to unexpected camera restarts.

According to recent reports, android consumers also get a handful of smaller, but welcome, fixes, like more reliable camera history controls, fewer unwanted Nest account-linking prompts, and clearer instructions on how to re-link third-party cameras. The ability to remove an offline, unmigrated 1st-generation Nest Doorbell is also returning.

#285. Latest Update: Contractor turns a Milwaukee Hackzall into a portable Ethernet untwister after facing job requiring 50,000 custom Cat6 cables

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Latest Update: Contractor turns a Milwaukee Hackzall into a portable Ethernet untwister after facing job requiring 50,000 custom Cat6 cables

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A contractor faced a project that required them to create 50,000 custom Cat6 cables from scratch, requiring 100,000 Cat6 terminations.
  • Industry observers note that his first solution to the problem was to buy a “Wire Straightening Machine” from Alibaba for $500.
  • It worked well at first, but he soon discovered that it was too bulky to use in the tight and hard-to-reach places where Ethernet cables sometimes terminate, like when you’re installing this heavy-duty outdoor Wi-Fi 7 access point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A contractor faced a project that required them to create 50,000 custom Cat6 cables from scratch, requiring 100,000 Cat6 terminations. The contractor, who goes by Analytical Horsepower on YouTube, had used a large, rare tool to streamline the job, but afterward he decided to build his own portable tool by modifying a Milwaukee Hackzall, cutting the time to straighten the twisted pairs to under two seconds.

Industry observers note that his first solution to the problem was to buy a “Wire Straightening Machine” from Alibaba for $500. It does the job well enough, but it’s an industrial machine designed for tabletop use, requiring an AC power source for the power brick and compressed air to run. The concept is that it clamps the wire between two rubber grips using air pressure, and then a linkage converts the rotary motion of the motor into a linear one, allowing the grip to untwist the cable. Since he wanted to use the machine in the field, he needed to make the thing portable — so he disassembled the entire thing, replaced the DC power brick with a 20V DeWalt battery with an adapter, added a push-button switch for power control, and a portable bike pump to deliver compressed air on the go.

It worked well at first, but he soon discovered that it was too bulky to use in the tight and hard-to-reach places where Ethernet cables sometimes terminate, like when you’re installing this heavy-duty outdoor Wi-Fi 7 access point. So, he studied the concept — it involved two flat, grippy surfaces grabbing the twisted cables and then moving back and forth. The back-and-forth motion of the surfaces causes the cables to untwist, with the clamping force ensuring that it remains in contact with the cables as they become flatter.

It has been revealed that with this, he realized that he did not need such a bulky machine to do the job — he just needed a reciprocating tool that could accept a clamp. He first looked at a reciprocating saw, but he found that it still had the same bulky problem and also called it “not overly precise.” But when he looked at the Milwaukee Hackzall, he found that it offered the perfect balance of portability and precision. More importantly, it came with a detailed data sheet, instruction manual, and parts breakdown that allowed him to accurately 3D print the plastic parts and laser-cut and bend the metal parts he needed to build his machine. He also used a toggle clamp to hold the Cat6 cable in place instead of a pneumatic piston, which further simplified the machine and cut its size and weight.

After a few steps of trial and error, especially in the quality of the grippy materials used for the clamping surfaces, he finally got it to work. He could reliably untwist softer copper-clad aluminum cables in one go in under two seconds. Harder 100% pure copper conductors, sometimes called solid copper or pure bare copper Ethernet cables, must be untwisted pair-by-pair, though, requiring a bit more time, but it’s still undoubtedly much faster and more convenient than doing the job with just your bare hands.

This tool isn’t worth it if you only untwist a few Ethernet cables every month or so, like this telephone-to-gigabit internet conversion job. But if you’re facing a massive job like Analytical Horsepower, that half a minute you save with every cable end could translate to over 830 cumulative hours of labor saved on the jobsite. It’s a great first-generation tool, with its practical use apparent in the YouTube video. Some commenters suggest extending the toggle clamp handle to reach the trigger so activating the tool is easier, while it also looks like a good idea if there’s a way to incorporate the entire system into a crimper.
