💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that samsung appears to be building a hidden Blocked calls dashboard inside the One UI 9.5 Phone app, according to Android Authority.
  • Recent findings suggest that blocking phone calls and automatically filtering out spam calls, are features that pretty much all modern day smartphones have.
  • This was discovered by the folks at Android Authority while digging into One UI 9.5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that samsung appears to be building a hidden Blocked calls dashboard inside the One UI 9.5 Phone app, according to Android Authority. It would show how many calls were blocked over the past 30 days, sorted into potential fraud, suspected spam, and numbers you blocked yourself.

Recent findings suggest that blocking phone calls and automatically filtering out spam calls, are features that pretty much all modern day smartphones have. But if for whatever reason you’d like to keep track of those calls, Samsung might be building a blocked calls hub. This will allow users to actually track all their blocked calls, maybe to check the numbers or to see the frequency.

This was discovered by the folks at Android Authority while digging into One UI 9.5. What they found was a dedicated Blocked calls dashboard inside the Phone app. It’s still hidden, so nobody can try it yet.

However, based on what they found and in the screenshots below, the dashboard highlights how many calls your phone blocked over the past 30 days. It sorts them into three groups. This includes potential fraud, suspected spam, and numbers you blocked yourself. So the next time you block a number from the new section, it will show up there the next time that number rings.

Industry observers note that that being stated, Samsung hasn’t officially declared anything yet. But then again, we shouldn’t be surprised. Samsung is busy working on new features for One UI 9.5. As with all these features, they are subject to change. So what we see now may look different upon release. Or in some cases, it might not even see the light of day.

Blocked-call history isn’t entirely new. Right now, you can open the Phone app, tap Recents, and use the three-dot menu to show or hide blocked calls. What changes is that the new hub would gather that information in one place.

Samsung also has several advanced call blocking or filtering features in place. For instance, the Galaxy S26 launched with a Call Screening AI feature. The firm is expanding scam call detection to more countries with One UI 9. It already offers fake AI caller detection in Korea. Google also previously launched its own Fake Call Detection in June.

In any case, this is just part of a larger picture. We’ve seen some of the other potential changes coming in One UI 9.5. The upgrade is expected to arrive early 2027, possibly alongside the Galaxy S27 series.

  • The first task is to power the Health app with AI to "analyze health information, such as sleep, exercise, and diet, and provide personalized solutions," according to the publication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, samsung and AI have become synonymous over the years. The company now says it wants to add more AI-powered support to its Health app to help users and medical institutions.

According to recent reports, today (Nov. 12), Medigate News (Korean) reported that Samsung is preparing major AI-driven overhauls to its Health app (via SamMobile). Samsung's digital vice president for the digital health team, Choi Jun-il, attended DHP 2026. According to Choi Jun-il, Samsung is preparing to "transform" the Health app "into a service." To achieve this, Choi states Samsung must tackle a few tasks.

The first task is to power the Health app with AI to "analyze health information, such as sleep, exercise, and diet, and provide personalized solutions," according to the publication. However, Samsung also wants to collaborate with established medical institutions in South Korea. Choi states Samsung has already started "opening up wearable sensor data to external companies with which we have signed agreements.".

Recent findings suggest that the goal is to standardize health data available through the Samsung Health app to deliver greater value to users. There's still a long road ahead for Samsung and its partner institutions, as the post indicates the organization is working on (and providing) proofs of concept with hospitals.

According to recent reports, in the U.S., Choi says Samsung wants to leverage its acquisition of Xealth. Xealth excels in digital health solutions for hospitals. It reduces the gap between the health data you capture on a Galaxy Watch and what your doctor sees and knows about you. Samsung says it wants to pursue deeper partnerships with U.S. hospitals through Xealth by 2030, potentially connecting consumers with over 100 institutions.

Industry observers note that samsung continues to push for better health assistance and insights, and I think this is totally worth it. If we're going to use AI to help, this is where it should be applied. It's even more worth it when you consider that your data will be shared with your hospital. This gets your doctor's eyes on your info, and they can make the judgment call that truly matters. Still a lot to be done, but this is interesting.

Samsung has more work to do on home soil to get to the same point as it is (or is going to be) in the U.S. Speaking of which, if all goes smoothly, Samsung would be able to transfer/share a user's "sleep, exercise, and blood pressure" insights from its Health app with their hospital.

It's no surprise that Samsung wants to bridge a gap between consumers and doctors. Last year, the company launched virtual doctor visits, which you can find in the app today. Through a partnership with HealthTap, the Find Care feature helps match users with a doctor for a virtual visit. Users can also text their virtual doctor in case upcoming symptoms appear.

#235. Dev hacks Coway air purifier to cut it off from the cloud

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (887 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Dev hacks Coway air purifier to cut it off from the cloud

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A developer discovered a clever way to cut his Coway Airmega IconS air purifier off from the cloud with the help of a root certificate, allowing local control.
  • Sources indicate that the developer, Scott J.
  • In a recent development, the fan’s inconsistency had a reason: the IconS has no official HA support, so the route around that relied on a community integration that logs into Coway’s IoCare+ cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A developer discovered a clever way to cut his Coway Airmega IconS air purifier off from the cloud with the help of a root certificate, allowing local control. The method took advantage of a security hole — the fan downloads the certificate over plain HTTP — and now his Home Assistant server stands in for Coway’s cloud. The result: no more dealing with the unreliable integration that ran through Coway’s IoCare cloud, which broke “at least once or twice a year.”.

Sources indicate that the developer, Scott J. Goldman, detailed why and how he did it, starting with replacing a dumb Airmega that was “an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor.” The replacement Airmega IconS, which is now discontinued but has Wi-Fi support, had inconsistent Home Assistant (HA) integration. He decided to take matters into his own hands with AI, although he noted that Claude’s guardrails blocked his request to set up his Raspberry Pi to intercept the fan’s traffic under the cybersecurity category, “not even for… uhh… testing purposes.” ChatGPT obliged and wrote the firewall rules, and an AI he doesn’t name later rebuilt the fan’s Bluetooth setup in about 20 minutes.

In a recent development, the fan’s inconsistency had a reason: the IconS has no official HA support, so the route around that relied on a community integration that logs into Coway’s IoCare+ cloud. Coway originally banned the integration for overloading its servers before allowing it after a community dispute. Coway also rebranded its app and cloud from IoCare to IoCare+, which forced a rewrite. Even small HTML layout changes on the pages the integration scraped could break it. On top of that, the organization’s servers went offline here and there.

Sources indicate that worse, the developer’s account was banned for running an old integration version, and he lacked remote control for weeks. Originally, all he wanted was for Apple Home’s Good Night scene to switch the purifier on. A common complaint about Internet of Things (IoT) devices like this is that you’re at the mercy of the manufacturer, and support can later evaporate. AI has helped some consumers like this take back control.

His method involved using the purifier’s security lapse against itself. At setup, it fetches the certificate it trusts over plain, unencrypted HTTP, which can be intercepted and replaced using mitmproxy/mitmweb with nftables port redirection. The request he saw was a plain HTTP GET for AmazonRootCA1.pem from an S3 bucket in AWS’s Seoul region. He then had his proxy serve its own CA to the fan, and the fan made HTTPS requests to Coway’s cert server, which included downloads of a device certificate and private key. Another proxy plugin then swapped his own key into that response.

It has been revealed that the fan’s commands ran over MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol common in smart-home devices, secured with TLS on port 8883 and routed through AWS IoT. The proxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it indicated the raw stream, which the unnamed AI mapped to his app button presses.

In a recent development, he had first considered exploiting eMudhra, a certificate authority whose private keys turned out to be trivially weak last month, which would have involved forging a certificate. That wasn’t necessary because of the plain-HTTP download. Self-signed certificates are nothing new to enthusiasts; this just took a little extra work and avoided the eMudhra initiative’s reliance on several things lining up.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Doing the Bluetooth work by hand would have taken hours or even days, he estimated. The unnamed AI also drove an Android phone over adb to read its Bluetooth logs and reconstruct the protocol.

Sources indicate that the project is offered as coway-local, which allows the fan to be connected to HA directly, and from there to Apple Home. A Web Bluetooth page, openable in Chrome on a Mac or Android device near the fan, sends the Wi-Fi details. That Bluetooth setup also carries the fan’s certificate URLs, so coway-local points them at the HA server and no traffic interception is needed. The Wi-Fi password goes to the fan over Bluetooth; HA never stores it, and the setup link expires after 15 minutes. The integration runs its own MQTT broker, so the fan now talks to HA instead of AWS.

HA Core 2026.10.2 or newer is needed with a fixed LAN address and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. There’s a catch: using it disconnects the fan from Coway’s cloud, so Coway’s app is no longer able to control it. It’s also experimental and tested only on the IconS (AP-1022K), and other Coway models may get through Bluetooth setup without actually working.

According to recent reports, the features list is incomplete: PM10 and other air-quality metrics, filter alerts, and firmware updates aren’t implemented yet. He suspects Coway’s cloud could eventually be discontinued or come with a service fee, and a local path is insurance against that. At least for him, this brings satisfaction, as “Now, I can finally click Good Night.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We've had quite the wait for the Tesla Cybercab to go from a promise made by company CEO Elon Musk to an actual reality, but following on from the introduction of the self-driving car as a robotaxi for the public, it's now available for individuals to buy too.

As per one of Tesla's accounts on social media, "select customers are now being invited" to buy a Cybercab "for personal use", though there's quite an extensive list of caveats to that — starting with that "select customers" part.

It has been revealed that there is no public order page, and Tesla isn't saying who gets invites or how. We do know prominent tech reviewer Marques Brownlee has an invite, quite possibly because after the Cybercab's October 2024 unveiling, he went on record as saying he'd shave his head on camera if it became available for less than $30,000 before 2027.

Industry observers note that the question of whether the invite-only system counts as 'available' is a sticking point here, as does the price. While it's $29,990 up front, there's also a $300-per-month subscription, which even Elon Musk has admitted is "too high".

It has been revealed that @MKBHD It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.November 14, 2026.

Sources indicate that there are other reasons why Brownlee's hair might be safe. The "estimated" delivery time is December, so if there's any delay on getting these to customers then the Cybercab won't have arrived for personal use before the end of 2026, invalidating the bet.

Then there's the geofencing. As you might imagine, there are only a few places in the US where fully self-driving cars are allowed, and at the moment the Cybercab will only function within those areas — specifically, a select number of cities in Texas and Florida.

As Brownlee lives in Latest York, he's not going to be able to use his new $300-per-month Cybercab to get around his home area — at least not until there's wider regulatory approval for these vehicles. Nevertheless, the celebrity YouTuber has gone ahead and placed an order to see what happens.

It's not clear exactly how many Cybercab robotaxis are in operation in Texas and Florida at the moment, but Tesla is clearly ramping up production and operations — and it might not be too long before anyone can get hold of one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

After adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

Industry observers note that there’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

It has been revealed that crazy to me that Google's own smart lock with Yale doesn't have this functionality. Seems like a huge miss for them to not be forward looking with their own hardware here.

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”.

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner.

In a recent development, the following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all users “over the coming weeks.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microbiologists at the University of Rochester modified an Ender 3 FDM 3D printer into a 3D bioprinter for engineered living material (ELM) research.
  • Recent findings suggest that synthetic biology is like combining engineering with microbiology, treating microbes as machines and physical building blocks to achieve various functions.
  • Sources indicate that the researchers kept most of the 3D printer's structure, mainly replacing the print head with a syringe pump mounted with custom 3D-printed PETG components, designed to utilize a 10 mL glass Luer-lock syringe with a plunger mechanism to control extrusion and retraction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microbiologists at the University of Rochester modified an Ender 3 FDM 3D printer into a 3D bioprinter for engineered living material (ELM) research. The team used SolidWorks to create the 3D model and sliced it in Slic3r, akin to a normal 3D printing workflow, with modified settings for the custom syringe pump print head. The $450 3D bioprinter makes ELM research more accessible, as bioprinters usually cost over $100,000.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic biology is like combining engineering with microbiology, treating microbes as machines and physical building blocks to achieve various functions. In the journal ACS Applied Polymer Materials, biologist Anne S. Meyer et al. published a 3D Bioprinting of Engineered Living Materials paper in August. The paper notes that synthetic biology and 3D bioprinting have advanced ELM research, but the hardware costs and the inability of the expensive hardware to maintain the structure limit further progress. Hitting two birds with one stone, the researchers built an open-source, affordable 3D bioprinter from an Ender 3 and created their own support slurry, allowing the ELMs to keep their shape.

Sources indicate that the researchers kept most of the 3D printer's structure, mainly replacing the print head with a syringe pump mounted with custom 3D-printed PETG components, designed to utilize a 10 mL glass Luer-lock syringe with a plunger mechanism to control extrusion and retraction. The workflow is very similar to normal 3D printing, with the shape created with CAD using SolidWorks, exported as an STL, and sliced in Slic3r. The researchers tweaked the print settings in Slic3r to match the 0.254mm needle, with the extrusion multiplier dialed down all the way to 0.004, resulting in a flow rate of 2 mL/h at a print speed of 23 mm/s.

In a recent development, instead of a filament, the researchers created a bio-ink from a mix of bacteria and alginate to be printed inside two types of support material: Agarose or gelatin gels. Agarose is used for long-term incubation, with the printed ELM staying viable for four or more weeks, and gelatin is used for extractable prints. The support slurries are enriched with Calcium ions, which cause the alginate strands to cross-link, creating a solid structure that encapsulates the living bacteria.

Industry observers note that ELMs are not limited to bacteria, but the paper mainly experiments with bacteria to explore bacteria-generated biomaterials with desirable characteristics such as biofilms for antimicrobial treatments, plastic degradation, or even wastewater treatment — or bacterial cellulose with structural characteristics to be used in applications such as a biodegradable plastic alternative. With the team’s efforts to make ELM research more affordable, developments could happen faster, with many applications across many fields, possibly even bacteria-based bioplastic 3D printing filaments for FDM printers.

#229. 007 First Light composers define a great Bond score by its ‘escapist elements’ — ‘A great game score should make the player feel like they are part of the story’

007 First Light composers define a great Bond score by its ‘escapist elements’ — ‘A great game score should make the player feel like they are part of the story’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained what they think defines a great video game soundtrack, in particular, a James Bond score.
  • In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the pair also discussed how they adapted their signature synth and acoustic hybrid styles to fit the traditional Bond aesthetic, Henson said, "We always look out for modern, thematic scores, with a unique take on action genres," to work with.
  • The Bond theme is one of the most iconic pieces of cinema music of all time, with Smith saying the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained what they think defines a great video game soundtrack, in particular, a James Bond score.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the pair also discussed how they adapted their signature synth and acoustic hybrid styles to fit the traditional Bond aesthetic, Henson said, "We always look out for modern, thematic scores, with a unique take on action genres," to work with.

The Bond theme is one of the most iconic pieces of cinema music of all time, with Smith saying the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond.".

"A James Bond score has to have all those escapist elements we talked about before," Smith stated, referring to "spy craft, intrigue, action and romance.".

As for a memorable game score in general, Smith noted the overall vibe needs to transport the player into the narrative and make it feel believable.

"A great game score should make the player feel like they are part of the story; giving atmosphere to the locations, humanity to the characters, and developing as they play through the story, the interactivity hidden but powerful," he explained.

The musical duo, known as The Flight, also believe that a score is another means to emphasise a game's story, with Smith saying, "A score needs to enrich and intensify the story and heighten emotional or exciting moments in the game.".

He added, "The music should also galvanise the player to move forwards and keep them entertained without being draining or too overwhelming.".

Henson continued, saying characters and locations always have their own recurring themes, which not only bolster the narrative, but also "gives familiarity" to the player.

"Game stories are likely to be completed over a matter of weeks rather than in one sitting," he said, "so this is even more notable to get the player swiftly back into the world after some days out.".

In the same interview, Henson and Smith explained how a young James Bond was "harder than it looks" because they had to avoid using iconic melodies before the player earned his 007 status.

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

#228. The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2478 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory.
  • Industry observers note that even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM.
  • In a recent development, but expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the organization’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Industry observers note that even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

In a recent development, but expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

It has been revealed that just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

It has been revealed that oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

In a recent development, I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

Recent findings suggest that at $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually released at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

It has been revealed that if you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

It has been revealed that I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a major thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon indicates that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

According to recent reports, we definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Significant Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

Sources indicate that droidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

In a recent development, now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

Obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

It has been revealed that with all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app problems, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

You might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software revision policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

Sources indicate that I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, revision (Nov 13, 6:57 am ET): Microsoft says recovery efforts are now in phases, with some affected infrastructure already back online and traffic slowly returning to normal. Initially, the company blamed high infrastructure loads across many regions, but the investigation eventually revealed a more specific problem with automated server health checks. The tech giant has revealed that automated server health checks misfired, kicking healthy infrastructure offline and triggering cascading connection failures across Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot. There are automated health checks that can detect failing hardware and take it out of rotation before your inbox breaks. Instead, a particular server component that does those checks started failing its own tests. Multiple regions lost their healthy servers, and the rest of the infrastructure buckled under heavier-than-usual loads, preventing users around the world from loading their mailboxes or sending messages. Now, Microsoft’s recovery playbook relies on working around its referee. Engineers made a targeted change to work around the faulty health-check component on some servers to see if they would stay online, while rolling out safeguards to stop other machines from dropping out. Automated recovery systems have been activated to minimize the disruption, and teams are also working in parallel to rebuild the affected servers with previous configurations.

Over a hundred thousand frustrated consumers were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

Outlook users in the Americas began reporting they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes, and the complaints were rolling in fast, with Downdetector reporting more than 125,000 complaints as of this writing.

If you attempted to refresh your inbox only to be greeted by infinite loading screens, you were not the only one. People are reporting being completely locked out of their accounts across desktop apps, web browsers, and mobile clients. Microsoft’s official 365 Status account confirmed the hiccup on X, blaming Exchange Online, the cloud backbone that powers your Outlook email, calendar, and contacts.

We're investigating reports of users experiencing challenges accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.November 12, 2026.

The organization initially mentioned the connection failures were limited to the Americas, but the company later confirmed that the connectivity bug could be hitting users in just about any region.

The problem is due to the way Outlook clients authenticate and connect to Exchange Online mailboxes using different connection methods.

Microsoft engineers are presently scrambling to resolve problems on the server end and mitigate the impact, but the company has not yet provided a concrete timeline for a full fix.

Apps in Microsoft 365 that rely on the same service connectivity may also be slow or throw error codes until the dust settles, though Exchange Online takes the biggest hit. For now, the best course of action is to keep an eye on the official Microsoft 365 status feed, enjoy a rare, guilt-free excuse to ignore your boss’s emails, and wait for the servers to wake back up.
